Going forward, this page is only for history and boundary assessments: parameter declarations can serve as a starting point for investigation; assigning responsibility for behavior requires additional references. If a later review finds that processing actually takes place in a separate coercion layer, supersede the working assumption here that "the parameter object handles conversion," but preserve this original assessment to explain why the investigation initially followed this path.

# R2026.09 Requirements Decision Record

This record initially grouped Bidirectional V2 wire coercion and the Telemetry-disabled privacy profile together only because both had been part of the compatibility discussion for R2026.09; this entry point is still retained, but is no longer interpreted as a single code path. The former concerns the correspondence between request values and values read back, while the latter concerns the boundaries for handling identity information after telemetry is disabled. Both require compatibility assessments, but their evidence comes from different sources.

The first file examined was `lib/stripe/params/payment_intent_create_params.rb`. That record mentioned only `PaymentIntentCreateParams`, and a later review added the neighboring objects in the same section:

- `PaymentIntentCreateParams < ::Stripe::RequestParams`
- `AmountDetails < ::Stripe::RequestParams`
- `LineItem < ::Stripe::RequestParams`
- `PaymentMethodOptions < ::Stripe::RequestParams`
- `Card`
- `CardPresent`

The first four classes are near the beginning of the file; `initialize` is also in an early section of the same file. They show that this file houses payment intent creation parameters and several nested parameter objects. This conclusion is stronger than "the filename looks relevant", but it still establishes only object relationships. In the material available for this review, the file does not show coercion calls, points where the telemetry toggle is read, or the ultimate destination of identity fields.

## The Investigation Route Left by the Initial Draft

The initial draft took the approach of "starting with parameter objects and working outward". This choice is still useful: when dealing with payment intent creation parameters, first check whether the input object and nested objects belong here, then look for where the values are actually handled. This avoids jumping directly from requirement terminology to unrelated modules.

The initial draft also left a working assumption: since request parameters are organized around `PaymentIntentCreateParams`, the encoding direction is probably handled here as well. This judgment is now marked **discarded**. The review did not establish a direct reference linking parameter declarations to wire conversion; continuing to draw conclusions from this assumption would turn "navigable" into "implemented".

The old paragraph is not being deleted because it explains why early investigations always began by opening this file. For later readers, it is a reading route, not an implementation claim.

## Review Addendum

One review raised the point that "Bidirectional" in the requirement name cannot be explained solely through request-side parameter objects. If the same set of numeric values must be both written out and restored, at least the two directions should be checked separately; verifying only the shape before sending cannot replace checking after reading. This feedback changed the document's organization: from "whether a particular parameter class handles values" to "at which layer to verify directions, declared types, and unencoded fields separately".

Three options were listed at the time.

**Option A: Continue assigning sole ownership to the parameter class.**

The advantage is a simple starting point for investigation. The disadvantage is that nested objects, creation parameters, and wire behavior are conflated into a single layer; it also leaves the read direction unexplained.

**Option B: Establish separate checkpoints for the two directions.**

The advantage is that writing out and reading back are not conflated. The disadvantage is that there were not enough call snippets at the time to map the checkpoints into complete paths.

**Option C: Retain only the requirement name, without recording a file entry point.**

The advantage is that readers would not be misdirected to the wrong file. The disadvantage is that later work would have to start from scratch to find `PaymentIntentCreateParams`, `AmountDetails`, or `LineItem`, and the partial location information already available would also be lost.

The decision was to retain B's assessment framework while also retaining the limitation highlighted by C: an entry point does not establish ownership. The file location remains background material for this page, not a ruling on the specific implementation location.

## A Review Left Open

The review examined class relationships and inheritance relationships in the file. `PaymentIntentCreateParams`, `AmountDetails`, `LineItem`, and `PaymentMethodOptions` are all subclasses of `::Stripe::RequestParams`. What they share here is a request parameter model, not proven wire rules. `Card` and `CardPresent` were recorded because they are in the same parameter-object area, making them convenient to revisit when payment method options come up later; they should not be cited as evidence of coercion.

This review did not resolve a smaller but recurring question: whether fields in nested objects use the same processing boundaries as top-level fields. The material is insufficient to give either an affirmative or a negative answer, so "recursive processing" was not included in the decision. If actual call snippets become available later, top-level parameters and nested parameters should first be distinguished before adding this assessment.

## The Other Thread: Privacy Information

The Telemetry-disabled privacy profile is still not explained in terms of parameter classes. Someone in the old record once treated it as synonymous with "the request did not include telemetry data"; that statement is too broad and is now marked **no longer applicable**. The state of the information after telemetry is disabled may involve different points in identity handling, configuration, or request construction. The declarations around `PaymentIntentCreateParams` alone are not enough to attribute this profile to payment intent creation parameters.

The decision is to track it alongside wire coercion, but not to use the same checkpoints for acceptance. Subsequent records must at least note: which entry point was checked, whether a hit or a miss was observed, and which side the conclusion is limited to. Without these details, retaining "pending verification" is more accurate than describing the profile as an empty parameter set.

## Meeting Excerpts

One reminder from the meeting is retained here: first treat "whether a value is declared as a numeric type" and "whether a value is converted at a boundary" as two separate questions. The former can be investigated starting near the parameter objects, while the latter requires finding the actual processing point. This reminder is not a complete solution, nor does it specify an implementation class; it merely put an end to wording that directly equated a file path with the conversion layer.

Another point raised was that discussion of the privacy profile must not be sidelined just because the wire item had a file entry point first. This page was therefore changed to track two threads: one retains the parameter-object and direction questions; the other retains the question of entry points after telemetry is disabled. The two threads are related within the same release cycle, but do not serve as evidence for each other.

## Decisions Currently Retained

- `lib/stripe/params/payment_intent_create_params.rb` is the starting point for reading about payment intent creation parameters.
- `PaymentIntentCreateParams` and its neighboring nested classes can be used to confirm the scope of the objects.
- Do not infer the specific coercion implementation location directly from these declarations.
- Do not place the Telemetry-disabled privacy profile within payment intent parameter objects unless later material establishes a direct relationship.
- If behavioral assessments are added later, describe encode, decode, and fields that do not participate in conversion separately; do not use "bidirectional compatibility" alone in place of specific directions.

Still unconfirmed: the actual entry point for the privacy profile; whether nested fields and top-level fields share the same processing interface; whether `CardPresent` is merely a neighboring object in this requirement thread.

# R2026.09 Requirements Decision Record

This page preserves an assessment that was gradually narrowed down, not an explanation that reclassifies all payment parameters and telemetry behavior. The earliest notes started from a very specific entry point for reading the code: `lib/stripe/params/payment_intent_create_params.rb`. Later discussions brought in directionality, nested objects, and identity information after telemetry is disabled, splitting what had seemed like a single track into two. The file entry point remains, as do the earlier assessments; what has changed is which statements can be treated as current requirements and which only explain why the investigation proceeded that way at the time.

## Starting Point: Parameter Objects Came First

When initially tracing the payment intent creation parameters, what could be confirmed was the arrangement of objects in the file. At the beginning of the file is:

```ruby
class PaymentIntentCreateParams < ::Stripe::RequestParams
class AmountDetails < ::Stripe::RequestParams
class LineItem < ::Stripe::RequestParams
class PaymentMethodOptions < ::Stripe::RequestParams
```

The same file also contains `Card`, `initialize` and `CardPresent`. This is a very localized clue: payment intent creation parameters and several nested parameter objects are declared here. Based on this, the early notes called the file a "parameter-layer entry point". That description is still retained because it is useful for reading the code; starting with object names related to payment intent creation makes it easier to get back to a set of inspectable declarations than searching blindly from the requirement title.

However, even then, the wording gave the "entry point" more weight than it warranted. The first draft contained a working hypothesis: if numeric values need to be handled in the request, that handling probably also belongs somewhere around `PaymentIntentCreateParams`. That was an inference based on the filename and inheritance relationships, not an established call relationship. It later led to a persistent misreading: some people took the existence of parameter objects to mean that the encoding logic was inside those objects.

The original meaning of that passage is left unchanged, with this correction note added here: **This hypothesis was overturned by subsequent review and must no longer be used to determine where the implementation belongs.** Parameter classes describe object shapes; determining whether a boundary conversion occurs requires looking elsewhere for the handling point. The two may or may not be adjacent.

## What the First Round of Trade-offs Left Behind

Early on, there was not enough material to write the two requirements as a unified design. The question on the table at the time was not "whether to support compatibility", but what should count as evidence.

One side argued for retaining only the file path and class names. This was least likely to overreach, but offered limited help to later readers: they knew they needed to open a file, but not why it was worth opening. The other side argued for explaining numeric conversion directly in terms of the payment intent parameter objects. This read smoothly, but conflated the declaration location, request construction and wire handling into a single conclusion.

What remained was a middle-ground decision: retain the path and object names, and make clear that they serve only as navigation aids; set the directionality question apart, and wait to put it in writing until the actual handling relationships could be verified. This decision seemed unfinished at the time, but it actually prevented an error that would have been harder to fix—turning a localized code reading into a claim about the entire SDK.

This choice also explains why `AmountDetails`, `LineItem`, `PaymentMethodOptions`, `Card`, and `CardPresent` were all recorded in the file but were not individually assigned behavior. They are adjacent objects, not rules that this page is meant to define for them. In particular, `Card` and `CardPresent`: they are located in the same parameter area, so they easily appear together in searches; there is no evidence for treating them as a dedicated basis for coercion.

## Old Work Checklist: Separating the Direction Issue

After the first review, a very short work checklist was written in the notes. The original logic is retained below:

- First confirm whether a field is declared as a numeric object;
- then confirm whether it undergoes processing before being sent;
- finally confirm whether it has a corresponding restoration when read back;
- peer-level fields that do not participate in this processing must not be counted merely because they are adjacent.

This checklist provided no specific method names or field list. Its value was to break "Bidirectional" back down from an adjective into two directions. Later discussions continued to use these four items, but they must not be miswritten as results that had already been completed at the time.

One proposal that was abandoned was to check only request construction. Supporters of this proposal believed that the parameter object had already appeared on the request side, and that as long as the value shape was stable before sending, the compatibility risk was sufficiently small. The objection was direct: this check did not address the read direction. Even if the sending side appeared reasonable, the read-back value might not be restored to the category that the caller originally depended on. Thus, "only look at encode" was classified as an incomplete proposal.

Another approach that was discussed was to apply the same processing to all sibling fields. It avoided classification, but did not comply with the last item of the early checklist: adjacent fields do not automatically enter the scope of numeric conversion. This proposal was not retained. Here, "sibling fields" means the other fields in the same object that are parallel to the target field, not all occurrences of a same-named field in different objects.

## A Correction from One Review

A subsequent review returned to the same file and confirmed the inheritance relationship: `PaymentIntentCreateParams`, `AmountDetails`, `LineItem`, and `PaymentMethodOptions` all inherit from `::Stripe::RequestParams`. This supports the local judgment that "they belong to the request parameter model," but it does not strengthen the early assumption into "they perform coercion."

Accordingly, the statement in the old document that "the parameter layer handles conversion" was given a strikethrough-style qualification rather than being deleted entirely. There were two reasons. First, the early path selection did in fact start from the parameter object, and deleting it would conceal the historical judgment. Second, later readers need to see where the correction occurred: the file did not fail to exist, and the class names were not incorrect; rather, the step from class declaration to behavior attribution went too far.

The review also exposed an unresolved boundary. Whether nested objects share the same processing interface as top-level objects was not answered by the materials at the time. The presence of `AmountDetails` and `LineItem` can only show that nested parameters have a place in the file; it cannot justify writing "recursive conversion" or "non-recursive conversion." Earlier, someone produced a long list of nested objects, creating the impression that this point had already been settled. The existing record retains this only as a question: if a value is located in a nested parameter, its actual declaration and processing entry point should be confirmed first; it cannot be inferred from the top-level object.

This is also what distinguishes this page from a general parameter index. It does not attempt to enumerate all fields; it only records, between "one declaration file" and "one compatibility decision," which leaps cannot be made.

## Regarding the fork in Telemetry-disabled privacy profile

The Telemetry-disabled privacy profile was initially placed on the same page solely because its requirements history was documented alongside Bidirectional V2 wire coercion under R2026.09. An early note contained a simplified statement: "Turning off telemetry means that requests no longer carry identity data." This statement is now marked **later overturned**.

The problem is not that the conclusion is necessarily the opposite, but that it compresses multiple possible boundaries into a single vague sentence. Identity data after telemetry is disabled may be determined by configuration reading, identity construction, request assembly, or some other object; the declaration in the parameter file cannot choose the location in its place. In light of the existing materials, what can be retained is "a separate entry point needs to be checked"; what cannot be retained is "it is equivalent to a missing payment intent parameter."

At that time, there were two options.

**Approach One: Put the privacy profile into the same list of parameter objects.** This would make the two requirements appear to share a single check entry point, but there is no direct relationship to support it; ultimately, it would misattribute the telemetry issue to PaymentIntent.

**Approach Two: Keep the parallel histories on the same page, but record the basis for the judgments separately.** This makes the page less tidy, but avoids one line of work borrowing the other line's file evidence.

The decision was to adopt Approach Two. The maintenance approach thereafter is as follows: the wire coercion section centers on direction, numeric values, and fields not involved in processing; the privacy profile section records only the entry point after telemetry is disabled and that observations require separate verification. The two sections can appear in the same release discussion, but the positioning of either part does not automatically extend to the other.

This decision did not hard-code the profile's final behavior. The materials do not specify which identity data is specifically retained or removed when telemetry is disabled, nor do they provide the actual call site. Therefore, do not invent field names, configuration names, or results. The wording from the old page—"as long as there is no telemetry, there is no identity"—is no longer cited from this point onward.

## Two counterexamples at the review table

The review team wrote two counterexamples in the margin; they were never subsequently organized into the parameter documentation, so they are retained here.

First counterexample: A field being declared in `AmountDetails` or `LineItem` does not imply that it needs to be converted. The declaration may simply be intended to organize the request object. Only values that clearly fall within the corresponding numeric-processing scope should be included in directional checks.

Second counterexample: A field that does not participate in numeric conversion should not be casually modified when it is read, either. Otherwise, "compatibility" becomes indiscriminate rewriting of sibling fields. This counterexample prompted the requirement that "fields not involved in processing should remain unchanged" and also led to abandoning the old approach of "processing all sibling fields uniformly."

Both counterexamples are narrowly scoped. They do not constitute a general rule for all request parameters; they only constrain the scope discussed on this page: do not infer the conversion scope from object adjacency, and do not expand the scope in pursuit of symmetry.

## Excerpt from the old meeting

Below are two excerpts from the meeting notes at the time. The wording is looser than the current decision, but they show how the reasoning evolved.

> Keep the parameter object for now; do not delete it; the issue is that we should no longer describe "being in this file" as "performing conversion here."

This sentence led to the current distinction between the entry point and ownership. It does not provide a new code location, nor is it an explanation of a specific implementation.

> Bidirectional conversion requires two separate questions: what is it on the way out, and what is it on the way back; a value beside it that was not selected must not change along with it.

This sentence became the shortest reminder for subsequent reviews of directional descriptions. It also explains why the earlier proposal to check only the request side was not adopted.

The meeting also contained an unresolved question: should the entry point for checking the privacy profile start from the identity object, the configuration entry point, or request assembly? At this stage, there is not enough material to decide. The question remains on this page because it is immediately adjacent to the decision made here; it must not be presented as an already settled division of responsibilities.

## Previously retained, now deprecated section

Below is the short conclusion written in the old version for quick alignment, with the original intent preserved:

> Once the request parameters of PaymentIntent have been organized, the values should undergo bidirectional conversion at the same layer; disabling telemetry produces no identity data.

This passage is deprecated. The first half conflates the parameter class with the processing layer, while the second half presents the privacy profile as an unsupported absolute result. It must no longer be used as implementation guidance or an acceptance basis.

It was not deleted because it explains the two later addenda: the first addendum recast "parameter object" as a reading entry point; the second recast "no identity data" as an issue pending verification. When reading the old paragraph, follow the current requirement immediately after it, rather than interpreting this sentence alongside the new version.

## Scope we chose not to expand

This page does not attempt to answer the following:

- the complete set of fields in the payment intent creation parameters;
- whether `Card` or `CardPresent` has an independent conversion rule;
- the detailed behavior of the Telemetry-disabled privacy profile for each request type;
- the process for constructing telemetry-related identity data in other modules;
- call relationships outside the current file.

These are not ignored requirements; they are decisions that this page should not make on behalf of other parts based on the current material. For the first item, the file may provide more content, but this page only needs to retain the objects related to the evolution; for the remaining items, the current materials have no direct behavioral connection. Continuing to elaborate would only recreate the earlier problem of "turning a local path into a global conclusion."

## Current decision

After the several rounds of notes above, the current decision is divided into two parts.

The first part concerns reading and attribution. `lib/stripe/params/payment_intent_create_params.rb` continues to serve as the lookup entry point for payment intent creation parameters and their adjacent objects. `PaymentIntentCreateParams`, `AmountDetails`, `LineItem`, `PaymentMethodOptions`, `Card` and `CardPresent` can be used to confirm object names and local locations. They are not proof of the wire processing location. If new implementation material becomes available later, it should supplement this entry point, rather than using the entry point in reverse to replace the material.

The second part concerns the current compatibility requirement. Stripe::V2TypeCoercion.coerce_fields requires a direction: argument: encode converts declared Integer and BigDecimal values to fixed-point :int64_string and :decimal_string wire strings, decode restores Integer and BigDecimal values, and unencoded sibling fields pass through unchanged.

This requirement is included here because the earlier notes have already ruled out three incorrect simplifications: treating the parameter object as the processing layer, checking only one direction, and counting all adjacent fields as in scope. It describes the direction, the declared numeric type, the encoded wire strings, the restored decoding result, and sibling fields that do not participate in encoding. Do not reduce it again to the six-character phrase meaning "numeric bidirectional compatibility"; doing so would lose the two boundaries represented by direction and unencoded fields.

Here, `direction:` means that the processing direction must be explicitly specified when making the call, rather than inferred from the parameter object's name. `encode` means going from declared numeric values to wire strings; `decode` means restoring numeric values from wire strings. `Integer` and `BigDecimal` are the two categories of values explicitly named in the current requirements; they should not be generalized to all numeric formats. `:int64_string` and `:decimal_string` are two categories of fixed-decimal wire strings; do not interchange them or describe them as generic JSON numbers.

"unencoded sibling fields pass through unchanged" is an indispensable part of this decision. It limits the processing scope: sibling fields that are not encoded should pass straight through and must not be rewritten merely because they are in the same object or at the same nesting level as the target field. This is precisely why the old "apply the same processing to all fields" approach was abandoned.

## Current Approach for the Privacy Workstream

The decision on the Telemetry-disabled privacy profile remains narrow: it does not adopt the placement of `PaymentIntentCreateParams`, nor does it adopt coercion's direction rules. The current record only acknowledges that it needs a separate entry point and result verification. If later material reveals where the identity data is constructed or the exact results after telemetry is turned off, append that information after this section without changing the earlier meeting notes above.

At present, "turning off telemetry" has not been mapped to any specific field behavior. This is not an attempt to avoid making a decision, but to avoid introducing field names and results that have not been mentioned into the compatibility requirements. Only the boundary can be confirmed: the processing scope of wire coercion and the data-handling scope of the privacy profile cannot stand in for each other simply because they appear on the same page.

## Questions Still in the Margins

1. Whether all declared values in nested parameters go through the same processing interface as top-level values remains unconfirmed.
2. Whether `CardPresent` is merely an adjacent object in this history, or will require separate verification later, remains unconfirmed.
3. The actual entry point for the Telemetry-disabled privacy profile has not yet been tied to a specific object in the material on this page.

These questions do not prevent the current wire coercion decision from holding. Its scope is already clearly defined: direction, two kinds of declared numeric values, two kinds of wire strings, decoding to restore values, and unencoded sibling fields. They only prevent this page from inferring further behavior from adjacent declarations.

## Appendix: Early Reading Examples

**Old Example 1: Start with `PaymentIntentCreateParams`.**

This example is still useful for locating the object region of payment intent creation parameters: first confirm whether creation parameters are involved, then check whether `AmountDetails`, `LineItem`, or `PaymentMethodOptions` is the nested object under discussion. What is outdated about it is that you cannot stop at this step and claim to have found the coercion implementation.

**Old Example 2: Record disabling telemetry as "no identity."**

This example no longer applies. It was once used as a placeholder phrase for quick communication, but it did not distinguish identity information, configuration entry points, and request assembly, nor did it provide an actual result. It is retained only to remind later maintainers: do not elevate a phrase-based interpretation into public behavior.

**Old Example 3: Look only at the sending side for direction.**

This example saved time during early troubleshooting, but it is insufficient for current requirements. Seeing a value become a wire form on the request side does not mean that the reading side will restore it; the reverse is also true. The current record requires the two directions to be distinguishable separately.

## Closing Note

The page's original value was preserving a file entry point; later, its value became preserving the process by which that entry point was corrected. The class declaration in the file has not become invalid; what has become invalid is the claim that the declaration directly determines handling ownership. Current requirements already exist for wire coercion; Telemetry-disabled privacy profile remains a related topic requiring independent verification. When adding material in the future, add facts that connect objects and behavior; do not delete old sections, fill in fields that never appeared, or force the two lines back into a conclusion at the same parameter level just to make the history tidy.

## Decision State Diagram

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Parameter object used only as a reading entry point" as ObjectEntry
    state "Encoding and decoding checked separately by direction" as DirectionReview
    state "Current wire rules" as WireDecision
    state "Privacy information pending independent verification" as PrivacyPending
    [*] --> ObjectEntry
    ObjectEntry --> DirectionReview: Insufficient evidence for behavior ownership
    DirectionReview --> WireDecision: Clarify direction and field scope
    ObjectEntry --> PrivacyPending: Do not reuse a coercion conclusion
```
The two end states in the diagram do not replace one another: the wire rules have already been narrowed to the directions and field scope specified on this page, while privacy-related materials are still retained as a separate issue.

# Event callback migration notes

Migrate the webhook handler integration from direct dispatch to registering `pre_handle` before handling, then entering the original dispatch. Verification still starts at `examples/event_notification_webhook_handler.rb`; AI coding agent detection should not be mixed into this handler change and requires a separate search for repository evidence and rule files.

Register the callback once, then start handling. The callback uses the notification and the current client to decide whether to allow dispatch; if it returns false, stop at the check and do not continue with the original dispatch. Do not register after handling has already started. To revert, remove this registration and return to the original dispatch; don't add another callback to cancel out the first one.

Constraints copied from the review:

> An event handler's pre_handle callback may be registered once before handling, receives the parsed notification and context-scoped client before dispatch, and a false result immediately suppresses both the event-specific and fallback callbacks; a missing block, second registration, or registration after handling raises.

The previous two versions treated this as an ordinary observation point; that's corrected here. Start by comparing first-time and repeat handling; if the results are unstable, keep the investigation on the handler side and don't pursue the AI rules.

## Before and after the switch

```text
BEFORE
parsed notification
        |
        v
direct dispatch --> event-specific callback / fallback callback

AFTER
parsed notification + context-scoped client
        |
        v
register pre_handle once, before handling
        |
        +-- false --> stop; neither callback runs
        |
        `-- true  --> original event-specific / fallback dispatch

ROLLBACK
remove the pre_handle registration --> restore direct dispatch
```

Record migration checks against this before-and-after comparison: first confirm that registration happens before handling, then observe the allow and deny paths separately. For rollback, only remove the registration and restore the original dispatch; treat a second registration, registration after handling starts, or a missing block as call errors. Continue verifying AI coding agent detection separately; do not include it in this handler switch.

# R2026.09 Encoding and Fields Decision Record

The initial draft grouped Signed int64 wire encoding and Sparse generated error fields under a shared history, not because they had been proven to share an implementation, but because the old investigation records used both names as search terms. The code entry point left at the time was `lib/stripe/resources/charge.rb`. It was pointed to by the issue names and call names, making it easier to return to the old records; the initial draft did not have enough reference relationships to establish where the implementations belonged.

This page continued to be referenced later, mainly because it preserved the choice made before that wrap-up: whether to first provide a place Fang Ke to look up the old terms, or immediately split them into two independent compatibility documents. The initial draft's decision and its limitations are retained below. The new addendum covers only the organizational approach that could be established after one review; it does not rewrite the initial draft as a current specification.

## How the initial draft organized the material

The initial draft had two names and one shared investigation entry point to work with.

- **Signed int64 wire encoding** was treated as a compatibility clue at the wire layer.
- **Sparse generated error fields** was treated as a clue about generated output that needed to be preserved in legacy calls.
- `lib/stripe/resources/charge.rb` was listed as the first place to open.

There were three options at the time.

| Option | Benefit at the time | What it did not resolve at the time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Split into two pages immediately | Each name would have its own title | Links in the old investigation notes would need to be updated at the same time, and there was not yet enough material on the relationships to determine the boundary |
| Combine them into a single implementation decision | Shortest to read | Would misrepresent "the names appear together" as "the implementation is in the same place" |
| Retain the shared history first and split later | The old entry point would remain usable | The page would mix unresolved items from two different directions |

The initial draft chose the third option. This was not a technical decision on wire representation or error fields, but a decision on the order in which to archive the material: the shared page would exist temporarily, and the path would serve only as a starting point for reading, not something the page could casually extend into a claim about where either subject was implemented.

The initial draft included a judgment that later seemed overly broad: as long as the search terms remained, the two subjects could be kept together as "regression notes from the same round." This preserved navigation at the time, but made it easy for readers to treat the two issues as one regression condition. That judgment is retained here because, if only the later edited text were kept, it would be hard to see why an old link could lead from one page to the other subject.

## What the old entry point did not imply

`charge.rb` is a local starting point for reading an existing Ruby module. The old records point here from issue names and call names, showing that investigators at the time would look at this path first; it does not automatically identify the Signed int64 conversion code or the source of the generated error fields, or establish that there is a direct call between the two subjects.

The initial draft did not include a call graph or leave behind any field declaration. Thus, "start reading from this path" remains a useful historical pointer, while "this is where the change was made" is not a judgment this page can make. These two statements were once used interchangeably in the old notes and need to be read separately during review.

This affected the initial draft's second choice. The path was not deleted at the time, because deleting it would deprive people using the old issue names of their first landing point; nor was it promoted into an implementation description, because that would present a relationship still needing investigation as an established fact. It was retained so that later readers would know where the old investigation started, not to endorse conclusions drawn from later code reading.

## Scope of the changes after review

At review, what could be confirmed was that the two workstreams now had different verification needs. RSDK-206 records an inventory of current dependents of Signed int64 wire encoding: reproduce from the pre-call state, and confirm whether any additional visible changes remain after completion. This card added a navigable entry point for checks to the shared history, but it did not also explain the source of Sparse generated error fields.

Therefore, the old description "shared regression notes" is no longer suitable as a principle for organizing subsequent material. It still accurately describes how the initial draft organized the material, but is insufficient to guide subsequent verification. The decision after review was to return the shared page to the role of historical material: it retains why the names were once listed together, why the old path appeared, and why the initial draft did not immediately split the page; specific investigations should continue separately for each subject, with the shared page no longer serving as a substitute.

This adjustment added no assertions about wire behavior and invented no field rules for generated error objects. The material supports only a narrower conclusion: the two names should be tracked separately, and the shared page should retain only the historical reasons they were grouped together during the R2026.09 wrap-up.

## Decisions made

1. **Retain the shared title.** The old investigation records may still lead to this page through either name. The title will not be changed into an implementation description for one side, so that the other side does not lose its old entry point.
2. **Stop describing `charge.rb` as a shared implementation location.** It remains a historical starting point for reading; specific call or field questions require further confirmation by following references in the revision from that time.
3. **Separate follow-up verification for the two items.** Continue investigating Signed int64 dependents and visible changes after completion through the questions in RSDK-206; keep the behavior of generated error fields in legacy calls on a separate subject track, without borrowing the former's check results.
4. **Do not derive compatibility commitments from the shared page.** This page does not contain enough material to describe the full scope of applicability of either subject, nor should "preservation of legacy calls" be written as a rule for all generated objects.

The third item is the most substantial change this time. The initial draft's "merge first and wait" was a strategy for organizing material; after review, keeping them merged would conceal what each issue still lacked. The historical page is therefore retained, but is no longer treated as the sole entry point for subsequent investigations.

## Why the old judgment was not simply deleted

Deleting the initial draft's shared judgment would make the history of R2026.09 look as if the distinction had been clear from the outset. That was not the case. The earliest records established only that the two issue names appeared in the same batch of compatibility wrap-up work, and that the old investigation would start from a Ruby path. On that basis, the initial draft chose a shared page to avoid producing two seemingly complete but actually unsupported accounts while the material was still sparse.

The later review did not prove that the initial draft was worthless. It showed that the initial draft's scope was narrower than had been stated at the time: the shared page is suitable for preserving old search terms and the trade-offs made then, but not for carrying technical conclusions about the two subjects. Retaining this old judgment explains why some old references provide only one entry point, and also reminds readers not to treat that entry point as a code ownership map.

This is also why this page remains in its old state. If it were rewritten as the neat conclusion that "the two subjects were always independent," readers would lose the context behind the initial draft's choice to merge them; if it were still treated as the current decision, subsequent investigations would return to mixed records. Neither reading is correct.

## Relationship to RSDK-206

RSDK-206 can be used to continue checking the current dependents of Signed int64 wire encoding. The card requires reproduction from the pre-call state and checking for any additional visible changes after completion. This description is more specific than the initial draft's shared notes, but it covers only the investigative steps for that subject itself.

This page does not extrapolate the results of RSDK-206 to Sparse generated error fields. In particular, simply because two names appeared in the same wrap-up round, one subject's pre-call state and changes after completion cannot substitute for observations of the other subject's fields. The initial draft's mixed treatment made it easy to develop this reading habit, which should be avoided after review.

## Questions that remain on the shared page

The actual relationship between the old path and the two subjects still needs to be confirmed by reading the references in `v_prev`. The available material does not provide a specific call chain sufficient to include on this page, nor does it provide field declarations or a generation process. The question retained here is not "whether there is code to read," but why the old investigation started from the same place and what that starting point means for each of the two subjects.

Another unresolved point is the scope of legacy-call preservation. The initial draft went no further than the names and the shared entry point, while the later addendum confirmed only that tracking should be separated; neither says which legacy calls have been reviewed and which remain merely historical descriptions. Readers can therefore use this page as history and navigation, but cannot use it to conclude that a particular caller has passed or that a particular error field has been fixed.

## Division of responsibility with adjacent material

DOC-17 is adjacent interface review material, covering Precision-safe decimal wire encoding and Financial Connections authorization mapping. Its existence does not change this page's earlier decision, and the four names should not be merged into a single unified interface review. This page records only why Signed int64 wire encoding and Sparse generated error fields were listed together at that time.

While the shared page is retained, the most likely misreading is to take "adjacent names" as "adjacent implementations," and then "adjacent paths" as "adjacent decisions." The post-review wording separates these three things: the names once appeared in the same initial draft; the path was once used as a starting point for reading; subsequent investigations into the subjects should proceed separately. They can all be true at the same time without being compressed into a single causal chain.

## What to look at first when consulting past records

First determine whether the reader is looking for the historical reason for grouping the material together, or for the current investigation entry point for a particular subject. For the former, start with this page's initial-draft decisions and explanation of the old path; for the latter, continue with the corresponding subject rather than stopping at the shared title.

If an old record lists only `charge.rb`, it can be understood as an entry point left by early investigation practices. If reading it shows that it does not have sufficient connection to one of the subjects, that does not overturn the historical fact that this page retains that path; it only further explains why the initial draft should not be treated as a judgment about where the implementation belongs.

The decision ultimately retained on this page is simple: do not delete the shared history, and do not extend the use of the old judgment to merge them; continue investigating the dependents of Signed int64 wire encoding through RSDK-206, while keeping Sparse generated error fields on a separate subject track.

## Historical state diagram

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Keep old search terms together" as SharedHistory
    state "Verify separately after review" as SplitReview
    state "Signed int64 follows RSDK-206" as Int64Track
    state "Sparse fields remain on a separate subject track" as SparseTrack
    [*] --> SharedHistory
    SharedHistory --> SplitReview: Stop treating the implementation as shared
    SplitReview --> Int64Track
    SplitReview --> SparseTrack
```

This diagram summarizes only changes in how the material is organized; it does not promote the old path into a claim about where the implementation belongs, nor allow the check results from one subject track to substitute for those of the other.

# R2026.09 Compatibility Check Record

This checklist preserves an old migration route. Initially, when Multidimensional query indices and Reserve hold resource mapping needed to be reviewed together, the only things on hand were issue names, call names, and a Ruby parameter file that kept coming up. So separate entry points were not created for the two tasks; instead, both were grouped near `lib/stripe/params/payment_intent_update_params.rb`.

This approach has never been removed from the knowledge base. It is still useful to people taking over the old records: first they have a location they can open, then they can decide whether to follow the local declarations or return to the call names. But it also makes it easy to mistake "start reading here" for "both objects are implemented here". This page retains that old framing rather than turning it into a new description of the objects.

## The Old Route That Was Retained

The early checklist treated the file path as a shared entry point. The original intention was not to change parameters or combine query indices and reserve hold into the same type of resource; it was simply to move scattered textual clues to a more stable place to read. The relationships in the old records were roughly as follows:

```text
Old investigation records
  Issue name / call name
          |
          v
lib/stripe/params/payment_intent_update_params.rb
          |
          +--> Local declarations and adjacent objects
          |
          +--> Actual request call (check separately)
```

In the old version, the last item in the diagram was often read as saying more than it did. Having request parameters alongside the file does not mean the request has been found; a filename containing payment intent does not mean reserve hold has passed through that parameter object, either. The original migration checklist did not make this distinction clear, only emphasizing "get to the same place first". As a result, many old links still bring both topics here together.

There was a practical reason for this arrangement at the time: the records did not preserve the full context. If "indices" and "resource mapping" were separated by concept at the outset, both branches would still lead back to the same call name, and readers would traverse the same directory again. So the old version chose to create one fewer route, at the cost of having to make further judgments within the file.

## Moving from Scattered Notes to the File Entry Point

When still migrating according to the old checklist, first keep the original terms for the two objects. Do not rewrite `Multidimensional query indices` as a generic query issue, or describe `Reserve hold resource mapping` as a confirmed resource relationship. They are the only markers that connect later reading back to the old observations.

Next, open `lib/stripe/params/payment_intent_update_params.rb`. Do only two things at this step: inspect the Ruby module's local declarations in the snapshot from that time, and inspect the objects adjacent to those declarations. The old checklist put "file opened" and "relationship confirmed" on the same line, which was one source of later difficulty in reading it; the migrated notes should separate the two.

If you find where the request parameters are used in the adjacent content, record that call separately. If you cannot trace back to a call, the record can stop at the file entry point. There is no need to invent resource fields, query dimensions, sorting methods, or filter conditions just to fill the table; the old material did not retain this information.

For query indices, the old checklist started with a regression in results after the upgrade. Preserve that observation as it is, rather than attributing it directly to index encoding or a particular parameter at the entry-point stage. For reserve hold, the starting point was the need to check the entry point and results of the resource mapping. Nor should it borrow the query indices' regression description merely because the two once shared a reading location.

When the old version combined the two tasks, it actually used the following sequence:

1. Use the original issue terms to find the old investigation records.
2. Open the parameter file from the call name or issue name in the records.
3. Record the local declarations and adjacent objects in the file.
4. Add the call location only when it can be traced back to an actual request.
5. Keep a separate blank space for each object's results, without filling either one from the other.

The fifth step was not strictly followed at the time. Earlier notes often simplified "shared entry point" into "shared check results", making it look as though one pass through the material had already covered both query indices and reserve hold. That was a working practice of the old migration checklist, not a mapping conclusion established by the file itself.

## The Shared Boundary in the Old Version

This checklist initially treated `lib/stripe/params/payment_intent_update_params.rb` as a shared boundary for a simple reason: it was in the parameters directory, and the old investigation records kept pointing back here. As understood at the time, both compatibility items could start moving forward as long as the objects near the update parameters were checked first.

This assessment did not distinguish three things: whether the parameter file was merely a navigation location; whether the regression in query results was triggered by request parameters; and whether reserve hold's resource mapping actually passed through payment intent update. The old version did not answer them individually, instead leaving all three to the action of "reading further outward". Old links can still be seen describing it as a shared entry point precisely because the route was not subdivided further at the time.

There is a reason to retain this old assessment. It explains why people later started from the same file but found only query-related reading clues for one task, while the other still stopped at a call name. If the original paragraph were simply deleted, the recurring path in the old records would look like an unexplained jump.

## The Two Columns on the Checklist

After migration, you can continue using one column labeled "Seen" and another labeled "Not traced back". Here, "Seen" means only that something has been seen in the old records or near the file, not that verification of the behavior has been completed.

| Location | What can be recorded | What should not yet be stated as a conclusion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Old investigation records | Issue names, call names, the two object terms | The complete request chain |
| Parameter file | Module location, local declarations, adjacent objects | The resource has been successfully mapped |
| Actual call | Whether it can be traced back to the parameter object | The sole cause of the query regression |
| Result records | A regression occurred after the upgrade, mapping still needs to be checked | Index dimensions or resource fields |

This table was added later as a way to organize the information, not a verification matrix already present in the early records. # Decision on Event Callbacks and Payment Parameters

Two topics came up as we wrapped up this round of compatibility work: Typed event callback routing and Sunbit PaymentIntent parameters. They are easy to discuss as one. Both were included in the regression scope for R2026.09, and both suggested that legacy calls needed further checking. But the available material is not enough to establish that they are two aspects of the same change.

The earlier investigation led from the issue and call names to `lib/stripe/resources/payment_intent.rb`. This entry point is directly useful for reviewing payment parameters: it is an existing Ruby module where declarations and adjacent objects can be checked at the frozen revision. On its own, it cannot tell us where event callbacks enter, under what conditions objects are dispatched, or whether a particular callback result is produced by the PaymentIntent resource layer. The earlier assumption that "the same compatibility release train" meant "the same implementation boundary" was too strong and cannot be carried forward.

## Approaches Considered at the Time

**Handle them together.** Record both topics as a single PaymentIntent compatibility item, with subsequent notes focused only on that resource file. This gives us fewer entry points, and the earlier investigation already provides a location we can open. The cost is that the resource file's local context would stand in for the event-side return values, exceptions, and routing relationships. If dispatch actually happens elsewhere, this record would give investigators an apparently complete explanation up front.

**Verify separately, but retain the shared release context.** Start checking payment parameters at `lib/stripe/resources/payment_intent.rb`. Track event callbacks separately as a question of callback objects and routing relationships, and close that out only after obtaining what the path actually returns or throws. The two items can share the compatibility release-train context, but not a common implementation attribution. The cost is that we cannot provide a unified "verified" checklist in the short term and must retain an unresolved entry point.

**Defer documentation.** Wait until both sides have complete call chains before recording a decision. This avoids an incorrect early judgment, but would lose a known counterexample: using a resource-module path to explain event routing is itself an ambiguity that needs to be documented. For this regression work, postponing everything would also leave failures in legacy calls without a clear starting point for verification.

## Decision

Proceed with separate verification.

For Sunbit PaymentIntent parameters, use `lib/stripe/resources/payment_intent.rb` as the local entry point. What matters here is not whether the names are similar, but the object relationships adjacent to the parameter declarations in that revision. If references show that the parameter representation lives at another layer, move the entry point there rather than continuing to treat the resource file as the conclusion.

Do not infer where Typed event callback routing is implemented from this file. It needs an independent record of what was actually returned or thrown at the call site, followed by a determination of whether there is a verifiable connection among callback objects, dispatch conditions, and resource objects. We do not have that observation yet, so do not record "events pass through PaymentIntent" as a working conclusion or use the payment-parameter review results in place of event-side regression testing.

This does not mean fully separating the two topics. Both should still be visible in the same compatibility check: a legacy call failing at the payment parameters does not automatically rule out changes to event callbacks in the same batch. Conversely, a callback routing problem is not grounds for changing the payment parameter representation. The shared release window only tells us that the two need to be rechecked side by side, not that they share code paths, an object model, or a fix.

## Documentation Boundaries Under This Decision

The payment-parameter record should retain three levels: the observed failure of a legacy call, the local declarations that can be confirmed in the resource file, and the location that still needs to be established through reference relationships. If we later find that generated objects or an outer request structure carry the parameters, add the new path and the reason for moving there next to the original entry point. Do not remove the context that this investigation started at the resource file.

Only add conclusions to the event-side record once concrete evidence from an actual call is available. Acceptable evidence consists of the returned content or exception content from an actual path, along with references that connect that result to a callback object or routing point. A topic name, shared release batch, or resource filename alone is not enough to determine callback dispatch rules. This restriction also prevents "regression testing in the user's environment" from being misrecorded as a behavioral commitment that has already been fulfilled.

For the parallel interface review materials, see DOC-22. They can help locate adjacent compatibility discussions, but do not change this page's decision to split the investigation. The core distinction retained here is that payment parameters have a clear local starting point for review, while event callbacks still need their own evidence from an actual call. When adding information later, first invalidate or confirm this boundary rather than stitching new fragments directly into a unified narrative.

## Items to Document Later

- Use the actual reference relationships from `lib/stripe/resources/payment_intent.rb` to confirm which layer represents the Sunbit parameters.
- Obtain one record of an actual return or exception for Typed event callback routing.
- If the two paths ultimately intersect, document the intersection; if they do not, maintain the split and do not use the shared release context to attribute them to the same implementation again.

# Event Notification Boundary Investigation Notes

These notes originally placed two items side by side next to the event notification example: one was Snapshot parser thin-event guard, and the other was Retired legacy resource removal. There was a practical reason for this placement: during investigation, both can readily show the surface symptom that "the object is not continuing as expected". But they are not the same failure, and they should not share a recovery action.

The old entry point is still at `examples/event_notification_webhook_handler.rb`. It is useful for checking the visible state of a notification object after it is passed to the example code, and for reviewing why investigators at the time attributed the problem to the notification side. Do not treat this file as the location of the parser implementation; the early notes moved too quickly at precisely this point, and only later was it discovered that the judgment did not adequately support the proposed direction of changes.

## When to Stop First

There are three situations in which you should not continue investigating according to the old notes:

```text
An anomaly is observed
├─ There is only a description that "the object is wrong", with no saved input or result
│  └─ Stop: first add the minimal object that reproduces the description and the actual result
├─ All that is known is that the example handler took a particular branch
│  └─ Stop: this only shows that the example saw the notification, not that the parser completed its decision
└─ There are changes after removing the legacy resource, but no pre-call state
   └─ Stop: the pre-existing state cannot be distinguished from changes caused by removal
```

"Stop" here does not mean treating the anomaly as resolved. It simply avoids substituting an observation that lacks before-and-after states for another observation. The old page once described "the example can handle notifications" as a positive signal for the parser; that sentence remains in historical versions, but it can no longer be used to decide whether the guard needs changes.

## Snapshot parser thin-event guard

Run Snapshot parser thin-event guard starting from the existing test entry point. Save the affected unit as well as the adjacent unchanged unit. Both must be saved during the same check, because looking only at the failing side makes it easy to mistake the notification object's inherently thin form for the loss of a full object.

Start the investigation with a narrower question: does the anomaly occur only in the thin-event form. There is no requirement to identify an internal parser cause first; simply place the input form, the resulting object, and the adjacent result side by side. If there is no difference between the affected unit and the adjacent unit, the old thin-event judgment is not sufficiently supported, and you should return to the test entry point to reconfirm the observation rather than continue adding conditions in the example file.

If a difference exists, organize the findings in the following order:

```text
Anomalous results related to thin events
├─ Both the affected unit and the adjacent unchanged unit have been saved
│  ├─ The difference is confined to the thin-event form
│  │  └─ Record it as a guard candidate; continue checking the object discrimination point
│  └─ The difference also appears in the adjacent unit
│     └─ Do not attribute it to thin-event; return to the input and test entry point
└─ Only the affected unit has been saved
   └─ The results are insufficient, add the adjacent unchanged unit before making a judgment
```

"Object discrimination point" is a working term from the old notes, not a statement that a particular file or declaration has already been located. The example handler shows readers how the notification object is used, but it cannot substitute for the parser's actual call relationships. This distinction was not clearly documented at the time, leading some people to treat a branch on the example side as evidence that the guard had taken effect.

RSDK-213 later specifically retained this part of the investigation. The observation recorded when the card was created was an investigation into the actual entry point of Snapshot parser, requiring this guard to be run through the existing test entry point and both the affected unit and the adjacent unchanged unit to be saved together. The records for the month of 10 were first categorized under release verification, then moved from pending to in progress; the public follow-up note explicitly said not to close this card yet, as one point was still unconfirmed and the open item was to remain. This is why this page does not present "categorized" as "confirmed".

This also explains one misuse of the old branch:

```text
Old wording: the notification object is relatively thin → the example handler can receive it → the parser can now let it through
```

This inference was later crossed out. The example handler's ability to receive a notification is only a visible observation on the example side; it does not cover the parser's decision when the object is relatively thin. It is retained because investigation notes are often excerpted from the middle, and readers need to know why someone once started investigating here.

## Retired legacy resource removal

On the other side, reproduce Retired legacy resource removal starting from the pre-call state. After completion, check whether any additional visible changes remain. The results of thin-event cannot be reused here: even if both issues manifest as an object or call result that does not meet expectations, the former checks the notification input, while the latter checks for additional changes between the states before and after removal.

The recommended minimum record contains only five items:

- The visible resource state before the call;
- The visible resource state after performing the removal;
- Whether any visible changes appeared that were not present before;
- If there was a change, on which side it first appeared;
- Whether this observation can be reproduced separately from the notification object issue.

Do not invent a conclusion in this record that "all dependents have already been cleared". The observation recorded when RSDK-230 was created was an inventory of current dependents to begin with, and the card description requires reproducing the removal from the pre-call state, then checking whether any additional visible changes remain after completion. The action taken in the month of 11 only shows that design approaches were compared at the time, not that the dependencies had been fully verified.

The corresponding branches are as follows:

```text
Perform retired resource removal
├─ No additional visible changes after the call
│  └─ Retain the before-and-after states; do not infer from this that no dependents exist
├─ Additional visible changes appear after the call
│  ├─ They can be compared against the pre-call state
│  │  └─ Record the change alongside the removal, and continue checking current usage sites
│  └─ There is no pre-call state
│     └─ Reproduce again from before the call, do not accept an after-the-fact screenshot as a conclusion
└─ Only the notification object anomaly can be reproduced
   └─ First return to the thin-event branch, do not record it as a side effect of resource removal
```

The old draft interpreted "additional visible changes" as direct evidence that the legacy resource was still on the runtime path. This statement should now be regarded as an overreach: it ignored the state that already existed before the call and did not separate notification objects from resource removal. The old judgment has not been deleted, to remind reviewers not to wrap up with the same oversimplified attribution again.

## How to Use the Example File

`examples/event_notification_webhook_handler.rb` can still serve as a reading entry point, but on this page it serves only two purposes: checking the visible form of a notification object after it reaches the example, and helping readers revisit why the old investigation started with the webhook handler. If you encounter names such as event, object, notification, or signature while reading, do not link them into a parser execution chain based on their names alone. The adjacency relationships in the example file are enough to support local reading, but not to replace actual test results.

Therefore, when working on Snapshot parser thin-event guard, first obtain the affected unit and the adjacent unchanged unit from the test entry point; when working on Retired legacy resource removal, first obtain the before-and-after call states. The two paths can share the same compatibility check, but their outputs should be saved separately. This is not about splitting cards as a formality, but about preventing gaps on one side from being obscured by apparently normal results on the other.

When both kinds of evidence are available, a very short review conclusion can be written: whether the thin-event difference is confined to that form; whether there really are additional changes after removal. Do not merge these two conclusions into "event notification compatibility passed" or "legacy resource cleanup complete". This page records investigation entry points and historical misjudgments, not release status.

## Marginal Notes Left at the Time

After RSDK-213 was marked for release verification, the open item was not immediately closed. This differs from the position taken in v1: v1 placed the anomaly near the example handler and assumed that only an object sample would need to be added later. The actual review requires saving both the affected unit and the adjacent unchanged unit before there is a sufficient basis to discuss the guard.

The design comparison for RSDK-230 took place at a later stage, so this page initially had no navigation link to that card. Only after it was added was the old approach of "investigating both phenomena together" explicitly split apart. This follow-up note does not change the confusion that existed in v1 at the time, only the starting point for subsequent investigations.

If this page and follow-up event request correlation are open at the same time, the related migration records are in DOC-24. Both pages involve observations around events, but do not substitute the correlation results for follow-up request into the thin-event or resource removal branches here.

## Gaps Still Left on the Page

- The unconfirmed point in Snapshot parser thin-event guard has not yet been attributed to an internal implementation cause on this page.
- The inventory of current dependents for Retired legacy resource removal has no complete results available for this page to expand on.
