# R2026.09 Interrupted Connection Handling

The initial draft put Interrupted connection disposal in the "Quality and Regression" category and recorded one small decision: when the earlier investigation points to `lib/stripe/resources/payment_intent.rb`, start with that file, without treating the path as establishing implementation ownership. This distinction is still worth preserving. Many later readers of this page saw only the filename and could easily misread "you can start reading here" as "handling after a connection is interrupted is completed here". The initial draft did not establish the latter.

The context at the time was also narrower than the title. There were no confirmed handling semantics here, only a repeatedly used issue name, an old source-code navigation point, and a requirement to return to the actual caller for verification. `payment_intent.rb` is an existing rb module that can provide local declarations and relationships to neighboring elements; it does not automatically establish how responsibilities are divided among the transport layer, response handling, and the caller. The initial draft retained this entry point so that the issue name would not lose its reference point in subsequent investigations.

## Choices in the Initial Draft

The first option was to treat the resource file as the direct location of the issue. This was the easiest way to write it: a path already existed, and the name was linked to the old record, so it seemed possible to immediately narrow the investigation to one module. This option was not adopted. When a file path and an issue name are related only for navigation, directly assigning ownership would lead subsequent readers to skip the callers they actually need to examine.

The second option was to record the path as a reading anchor while leaving judgments about behavior open. This was the option the initial draft adopted. It at least established a place that readers could repeatedly return to, without pretending to already know where the connection interruption occurs, who detects it, who cleans up, or whether cleanup succeeds.

The third option was to retain no decision and wait until all the material was available before writing it up. This was not adopted either. The earlier investigation had already linked the issue name and the call name to this module; removing this layer entirely would make the next reading start from scratch and obscure the fact that an earlier attempt to locate the issue had already been made but not brought to a conclusion.

So the decision in the initial draft was not "the handling belongs to payment intent", but "use the payment intent file as a reading anchor for now". This decision governs only how the record is written, does not replace a conclusion about the implementation, and does not mean the file should be modified.

## The Retained Earlier Wording

In the initial draft, "near the resource module" was used too casually. What that sentence originally meant was: first open `lib/stripe/resources/payment_intent.rb`, then check the object names and surrounding declarations referred to by the old record. It was later taken as a stronger suggestion, as though examining the resource layer alone were enough to establish where Interrupted connection disposal takes place.

That implication no longer applies. A path provides only local navigation; even if related objects exist in the file, that does not establish the order of handling after an interruption, connection ownership, or relationships to response handling. The old sentence is retained because it explains why this page originally started with that file; it should no longer be treated as the endpoint of the investigation.

The old record provided neither usable call edges nor results from a completed review. The initial draft therefore left "find callers still using this handling approach" as a follow-up action. This gap is not a wording issue: without the caller's actual version, entry path, and current result, the filename can only be a clue, not support a judgment about the implementation.

## October Addendum

RSDK-216 moved into an in-progress state on 2025-10-01. This action brought the old record back to light, but did not change the scope of the initial draft's evidence. The review addendum on the following day explicitly noted that one point in the HTTP transport and response handling section remained unconfirmed. The "remained" here matters: it neither rules out the resource file nor confirms any particular implementation, but instead marks a gap in what had previously appeared to be a continuous line of reasoning.

On the same day, the item returned to the to-do state, with the recorded reason that dependencies were not yet ready. This status change should not be read as meaning the issue had disappeared. It only shows that the required verification could not be continued to completion at that time. This is precisely where the earlier approach of treating the file path as the main reference point exposed its limitations: if judgments about connections still span an unconfirmed part of transport and response handling, focusing only on the resource module will not fill in the missing dependencies.

This addendum did not provide a new, complete technical conclusion. It only corrected the direction in which the initial draft might lead readers: `payment_intent.rb` cannot be treated as an alternative entry point to HTTP transport and response handling, nor can local findings from reading the resource side be expanded into a conclusion about the entire handling chain.

The timeline is retained below for reference when looking up earlier statuses:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> InitialRecord
  InitialRecord --> UnderReview
  UnderReview --> ToDo: Dependencies are not yet ready
```

In the diagram, "UnderReview" corresponds to the stage when work resumed at the time, and "ToDo" corresponds to the subsequent state after the item was put back in the queue. It does not mean the review was complete, much less that the dependencies became ready later.

## What Still Needs to Be Verified

The local requirement from RSDK-216 is: find a caller still using "Interrupted connection disposal" and verify its actual version, entry point, and current result. All three should be recorded together, rather than finding a seemingly relevant fragment for each one separately.

The actual version identifies which code version or dependency combination the item being checked actually comes from. Without this, the path in the old record may just be a navigation reference left over from an earlier version. The entry point identifies where the caller enters the relevant behavior; it cannot be replaced by the file path for `payment_intent.rb`. The current result should correspond to this version and this entry point, rather than a description based on impressions from a different call scenario.

That is also the full extent of the responsibility boundaries currently defined on this page: the resource module's path provides the old navigation reference; the caller material explains actual use; the unconfirmed part of HTTP transport and response handling remains unconfirmed. None can stand in for another.

If the caller found only shares the same name but has a different actual version, it cannot be used to infer retroactively that the old record was correct. If the objects encountered along the entry path have no direct relationship to the resource file, a connection back to that path should not be forced just to preserve the initial draft. Conversely, even if the caller ultimately passes through a resource object, it is still necessary to explain separately which neighboring part is responsible for handling after the interruption; "passing through" is not "being responsible".

## Decisions Made on This Page

Two decisions remain in place.

First, continue retaining `lib/stripe/resources/payment_intent.rb` as a reference point for revisiting the earlier investigation. This point is in `internal/ruby-sdk-evolution`'s `v_prev` navigation materials, and is a useful place for readers to reconstruct why the old record started here.

Second, do not use this path to affirm or reject implementation ownership of Interrupted connection disposal. Only after the caller's actual version, entry point, and current result have been laid out side by side can a separate judgment be made about the relationships among the resource layer, transport layer, and response handling. RSDK-216 is the navigation card for this verification; changes in the card's status cannot replace the verification itself.

This is not deferring the decision indefinitely. What has already been settled is the boundary of the record: the file path does not establish facts about calls, the unconfirmed transport/response handling section does not establish conclusions about the resource module, and dependencies that are not yet ready should not be recorded as a completed review. The remaining technical judgments still need to come from specific callers.

## How to Use the Old Entry Point

When revisiting the investigation, first use the old path to restore the context, then return to the actual point of use. If the reading reveals only resource definitions or adjacent declarations, record that as a local observation in the resource file; do not use it to fill in the process of connection acquisition, exception propagation, or response release. If the material only shows that a caller is still using the issue name, record only that it is still in use, and do not rewrite "use" as "has triggered the same behavior".

The initial draft did not require a list covering all callers. This page does not add that requirement either. What is currently needed is a verifiable caller sample to determine whether the old path still has explanatory value. Without a sample, the most honest status remains: the old entry point can be consulted, and the behavioral relationships are undetermined.

This page therefore remains a record of an earlier decision, not current operating instructions. Readers who only need to confirm why the earlier investigation led to the payment intent resource file can find the answer here; those who need to confirm the actual handling after a connection is interrupted must continue investigating with caller material in hand. After the October addendum, the former question still has a stable entry point, while the latter remains unresolved by this document.

# Short Checklist for Closing the Quality Signal Desk Window

This page is still the short checklist used at the end of a window. It has been kept because, during several reviews, people first asked where the last test output was and whether the borrowed entry point had been returned, rather than about the full release process. It covers this small slice of work around test: failure samples, regression stratification, and attribution of unstable signals; other release decisions are not filled in here.

The old version's three-line prompt is still retained: first find `generated namespace`, if you see `autoload boundary`, do not clear the working state, and stop if `compatibility window` is missing. They were markers used at the time to identify the window's position, not status names that every entry point provides now. Do not treat them as completion signals just because they appear in old records.

## Follow this order before closing the window

1. [ ] Pin down the current entry point for this run. Write the actual borrowed entry point, the purpose of the borrowing, and the latest return time next to the window record; if the entry point has changed, retain the one from before the change, rather than keeping only the one that later worked.
2. [ ] Keep the final output. Retain one raw output for each of the success and rejection paths, and do not overwrite failure samples while organizing them. List only the regression layers actually compared in this run; if an unstable signal has not yet been attributed, mark it as unattributed, and do not borrow conclusions from elsewhere.
3. [ ] Check the exit action first, then perform the rollback. If the normal entry point cannot reach the exit action, or if the exit action completes only a partial recovery, stop the closeout; do not record the manual cleanup after an entry-point rejection as a successful rollback.
4. [ ] After removing this round's bypass, confirm that no new test continues to enter this window segment. If new work is still coming in, keep the bypass and working state in place, wait for it to stop naturally, and then return to this item.
5. [ ] Return the borrowed entry point and hand the incomplete failure samples to a specific owner. You may mark this round's window as closed only after the return is complete and the rollback entry point has been fully completed.

## Where to stop when there is a fork

When the two sides' `stripe-quality-signal` revisions do not match, do not first choose the side that looks greener. Fix the input for this checklist and compare only the two revisions; if the generation command or time differs during comparison, stop at the first fork. The RSDKA-013 pair records the entry point where the revisions differ, and the RSDKA-016 pair records the stopping point when the two records are compared; neither is meant to choose on someone else's behalf which record should be treated as authoritative.

A record of a single-environment reproduction was later added for RSDKA-003, so a single reproduction may be attached after the failure sample, but it cannot replace the comparison with the other side. RSDKA-010 previously warned that the exit entry point and rollback status might be inconsistent: when the normal entry point is rejected at step two, the working state should remain "rollback incomplete," rather than adding a seemingly identical action just to close the window.

## Minimum record for the rollback entry point

- [ ] Which current entry point the rollback starts from;
- [ ] Whether the last output can still be matched to that entry point;
- [ ] Whether the borrowed object has already been returned;
- [ ] Whether it stopped before the exit action, or partial recovery was discovered after the exit action.

The old version once stated "after seeing `autoload boundary`, do not clear the working state" in absolute terms. This sentence is retained to explain why the raw output was kept at the time; it does not mean that all adjacent entry points must be judged using the same marker. If work outside the window encounters a marker with the same name, return to the record for adj-stripe and do not expand the handling scope from this short checklist.

## Supplemental note left during record comparison

The single-environment reproduction for RSDKA-003 has an easily overlooked prerequisite: keep the source code and command unchanged; switch only to another environment, rerun, and record the revision at that time. It is suitable for showing whether the same failure sample can still occur, but not for determining priority between the two records. If the rerun output contains only green results, it should still be placed alongside the original failure sample; the later result cannot be used to overwrite the first visible result.

When both records are laid out on the desk, first fix the checklist input, then look at the revision for `stripe-quality-signal`. If the revisions already differ, the comparison can go no further than this; if the revisions match but the generation command or generation time differs, record only the first fork. Later differences were not traced item by item on this page. It is inaccurate for the old checklist to group them all as one issue from the same round, but the stopping point from that time is still useful.

The exit action is a separate, independent check line. In the records for RSDKA-010, the normal entry point was rejected at step two; this only shows that the entry point did not reach the exit action. It does not show that the rollback entry point itself is usable, nor that the borrowed resource has been returned. Earlier, writing "rollback status" as a single term would mix partial recovery into a complete rollback. The original wording is retained now so that reviewers know why the window was not closed directly at the time.

The closeout record does not require all failure samples to be reattributed. Unattributed signals remain next to this round's output, and completed single-environment reproductions are marked only with their corresponding environment and revision. title: Postmortem: rbi caller integration record merge anomaly

versions.body:
# Postmortem: rbi caller integration record merge incident

The integration records showed two revisions, but the entry point displayed only one current revision. When the nested request schema was first checked against the old records, the differences were treated as changes to a single sample; only after revisiting the entry point was it confirmed that both sets of records had ended up in the same place. Readers could not tell from the entry point which set of fields to use as the reference.

The incident occurred between record archiving and later review. The request itself was not judged to have failed here. The problem was that the earlier assessment, later findings, and still-unknown scope of adoption were presented together at the same entry point. Reading on from the latest record would make the contents of the two revisions look like one continuous history.

### Timeline

- The first recorded observation was that the nested request schema did not match the old records. At the time, there was not enough information to distinguish the records, so this could only be logged as a sample difference. It was not possible to tell whether the difference came from the request structure, record version, or caller context.
- It was then confirmed that the entry point held two revisions at once. The old records had not been moved, so the entry point was still accessible on the surface; what was actually missing was a way to trace back from the entry point to the corresponding revision.
- No further retries were used to look for an explanation. Even if new output appeared again, it could only add material under the same entry point, not resolve the mixing of old and current records, so further retries were stopped first.
- The document version from that time was preserved at `docs/adj-rbi/incidents/rbi-client-integration-two-unmerged-record-versions.md`. It was kept so that later checks could still see the state of the entry point at the time, rather than replacing the initial assessment with the results of a later cleanup.

### Impact

The confirmed impact is limited to reviewing caller integration materials. Someone who needs to compare the nested request schema may retrieve records from the other revision and interpret field differences as changes to the current request. Conclusions drawn this way cannot be used to judge whether a particular request sample has already been adapted, nor do they show that fields in the old records will still appear in the current request.

The scope of impact has not been extended to all adopters. The available material does not list which adopters completed their checks using the mixed entry point, nor does it retain a record of which set of records was selected on each visit. This incident therefore cannot be described as affecting all callers; all that can be confirmed at this point is that the entry point itself cannot reliably distinguish the two versions.

### Actions taken at the time

Recovery started with the records, rather than adding an explanation on the caller side. After the fields that were explicitly present were tracked individually, explicit field tracking could be restored: fields under the same entry point could finally be mapped back to their respective revisions, and comparisons of the nested request schema no longer had to rely on the order of the old paragraphs.

This restored the ability to distinguish versions, not an explanation for every difference. Explicitly recording a field only shows that it appeared in the corresponding material; it does not prove that missing fields were deleted, nor does it supply the current revision with request context that the old records had never retained.

At the time, the context-scoped client was not identified as the cause. The change to it was noticed at the same time as the mixing at the entry point, but the available records cannot establish who changed it, where the change fell relative to the two revisions, or whether it directly caused the schema differences. This was left as an unknown, rather than using the entry-point issue as a substitute for the root cause.

### Assessment after recovery

The entry point can continue to serve as a navigation point, but anyone reviewing the records must first identify which revision they belong to, then compare the nested request schema. The old records can still be kept because they reflect the request samples from that time; they must no longer be combined with the field descriptions for the current revision into one continuous account.

The decision to stop retrying still stands. Retries are useful for checking whether a request returns consistently, not for distinguishing historical records that have already been mixed together. Without new revision markers or field tracking, adding samples will only make the two sets of material under the entry point harder to separate.

### Remaining work

The scope of adoption has not yet been verified case by case. Which callers obtained records from this entry point, and whether they used those records to assess the nested request schema, still need to be established; there is not enough material yet to pin down that scope.

No conclusion has been reached on the change to the context-scoped client either. If request samples separated out by the two revisions can be found later, the correspondence between the client context and the explicitly recorded fields should be checked first, before deciding whether this was merely a concurrent change or needs a separate incident record.

During the public entry point maintenance window, the results shown by the entry point did not match the original plan. After discovering the discrepancy, the on-call team did not proceed with the remaining maintenance as originally planned. Instead, they first checked whether the old entry point could still be removed. This sequence reflected the assessment at the time: as long as the old entry point remained, the public entry point's state could not be aligned with the window's plan. Before the removal, the records did not contain enough information to tell whether the discrepancy had already existed before the window started or had appeared during the window.

After the old entry point was removed, the public entry point returned to the state expected at the time. This was a temporary recovery, not confirmation of the root cause. The recovery action showed that the old entry point could still affect the entry point's results, but did not establish why it had remained during the window or at exactly which maintenance step the original plan had stopped governing the work. When reviewing the records later, keep "recovery" distinct from "the cause is known."

During recovery, notes were added on the actual impact, the coordinator, and whether the old entry point could be removed. These details had not been captured as directly checkable entries in the initial window records. As a result, when the plan specified an expected result but the entry point showed a discrepancy, the responders could only act on the visible state first. The added notes did not close the gaps in this record; they only preserved the rationale for prioritizing removal at the time.

At one point, the on-call team classified the issue as "the old entry point was not fully removed." That assessment remains on this page because it explains the approach taken for temporary recovery; it should not be read as the final attribution of cause. Removal can eliminate the visible discrepancy, but it did not establish the conditions that caused the old entry point to remain visible, nor did it rule out the possibility that other maintenance actions during the window changed the entry point's results.

During the investigation, searches were made using `lib/stripe.rb` and the call name `request_params`. This record only reflects the search path used at the time: the responders tried to find leads connected to the entry point's state, starting from the known file location and call name. That location was not confirmed as the permanent home of the public entry point; this postmortem is still about the entry point state discrepancy during the maintenance window.

The raw execution records should continue to be kept with this page. They contain the results visible at the time, the removal action, and control points added to the record after the fact, not a complete explanation of the cause. If material is added later on when the discrepancy appeared or on related actions, it should be placed alongside the old assessments preserved here, so it remains possible to reconstruct why removal happened and what was still unknown at the time.

Two things remain unconfirmed: whether the discrepancy already existed before the window started or was introduced by the maintenance process; and whether other maintenance actions were simultaneously changing the entry point's results before the old entry point was removed. The available records only support treating the removal of the old entry point as a recovery action; they do not justify narrowing this down to a single cause.

# Public Entry Point Maintenance FAQ

These three questions were recorded together next to the transport-runtime entry point at the time: what the entry point can tell us, who's responsible for withdrawing a candidate path, and when to close.

For now, use the rule "having an entry point means having public coverage." If the entry point exists, assume callers can reach it; no separate search for counterexamples was done.

## Who withdraws candidate paths?

Start by having the person who proposed the candidate path handle it. If the path ends up unused, the entry-point side doesn't need to retain an explanation, to avoid turning a branch under discussion into a long-term agreement.

Close once the existing regression tests pass. Loading boundaries and downstream chains are for each module to check and aren't covered in detail in these three questions.

# Public Entry Point Maintenance FAQ

This page was once used as a quick reference for public entry points and was later pulled up again because the three earlier short answers conflated "seeing an entry point," "withdrawing a candidate path," and "being able to close" into one thing. The old wording was not deleted: it explains why some discussions reported only the entry point and a regression and assumed the work was finished.

DOC-50 are adjacent single-variable rerun records. A rerun record only tells us what that rerun left behind; it does not assign ownership of the candidate path or fill in the execution history missing from this page.

## transport-runtime What Can the Entry Point Prove

It can prove that the candidate path under discussion has an existing public entry point available for review. The earlier answer described this step as "an entry point means public coverage" and skipped the negative cases on that basis; that judgment did not hold up later. The existence of an entry point does not mean the positive case has completed successfully, nor that the loading boundary has been examined.

Therefore, the entry point is the starting point for review, not closure evidence. If all we have is the entry-point location and one regression result, this page still cannot establish that callers will use the path. This concerns the team's judgment about maintaining public entry points; it should not be turned into a different kind of question just because of a repository filename.

## Who Is Responsible for Withdrawing the Candidate Path

The old answer said, "The proposer withdraws it themselves." It works for very small experiments, but leaves out cross-module chains: the proposer can withdraw their own candidate implementation, but cannot stand in for downstream's judgment that the path is no longer being used.

This page has no original execution record that can confirm who actually performed a particular withdrawal, nor enough material to assign candidate paths wholesale to the entry-point side. The narrower boundary we can retain is this: when a cross-module chain is involved, confirmation from the downstream owner cannot be omitted. Who performed a particular withdrawal remains unknown; do not infer a definite division of responsibility from the old answer.

## Under What Conditions Can It Be Closed

The earliest rule, "passing the existing regression is enough to close," has been deprecated. The later standard was: each change can be closed only after the positive and negative cases for its corresponding public entry point, the existing regression, and the loading boundary have all been reviewed; cross-module chains also require confirmation from the downstream owner.

This standard does not mean that every issue goes through the same set of checks. It only corrects the part of this page that originally gave too much weight to entry points and regressions. Follow-up questions where no original execution record exists can be logged, such as who reviewed a particular negative case at the time or which operation included the downstream confirmation; when records are missing, the answer is explicitly left unknown.

## Old Uses That Can Still Mislead

If someone only needs an entry-point location, they may still read the first half of this page as implying that the entry-point side can close things on its own. That is exactly why this page was not updated as current operating instructions. The old FAQ is retained for looking up historical decisions; before closing, review each item against the later standard above rather than citing the initial three short answers.
